## Discussion

In this paper we have presented a joint model of the size of the 2026 Bundibugyo virus outbreak fitted to every count the national situation reports publish.
At the release analysed the joint estimate sat below every single-stream fit.
The one-week-ahead forecasts rarely beat a persistence baseline, and the onset reports were the only stream on which they beat it at most releases.

<!-- Strengths and limitations -->

The approach has several strengths.
First, one posterior over every published stream shows where the streams agree and where they disagree, and resolves that disagreement inside the model.
Under the renewal model that disagreement appears to be absorbed by the ascertainment and background terms, while under the laboratory model it inflated the size estimate above every single stream.
Second, fitting the cumulative counts as increments with a level offset at each documented change handles revisions and format changes rather than ignoring them.
Third, each release with a scored successor was tested against the data that arrived next, so those forecasts met a test outside the window they were fitted to.
Finally, the whole model definition lives in one versioned document that others can review and adapt, and it is refit and released with each data update.

The main limitation is that the delays, the case-fatality ratio and the laboratory parameters rest on priors from other outbreaks or from judgement.
The data do little to move them, so the size interval inherits their width and any error in them moves the estimate the same way.
Almost every count is report-dated, so the timing of the epidemic is recovered through those assumed delays rather than observed.
At the release analysed the generation-interval prior was wider than documented, and the fitted mean sat far below the serial interval the prior was centred on, which feeds into every reproduction number reported here. <!-- PRs 907 and 909 -->
The reproduction of the first model has not been checked against the original authors' code.
The data are aggregate national and provincial counts, with no line list in the released model.

The streams share one case pool but are treated as conditionally independent given the latent infections, which may understate the uncertainty in the joint estimate.
The fitted streams may look sub-exponential while the reproduction number sits above one, so the model may misstate growth over the window. <!-- Sebastian, issue 243 -->
The forecast intervals covered nearly every observation, so they are too wide to separate one plausible week from another.
However, the aggregate design still supports the per-stream ascertainment and the forecast evaluation reported here.

<!-- Comparison to the literature -->

Each published estimate answers a different question from a different subset of the published counts.
The reproduction of the method of McCabe et al. [@mccabe2026] at their own fixed inputs recovers their headline estimate, and the joint posterior sits above both of their headline scenarios and overlaps only the upper half of their back-calculation scenarios at the matched cut-off.
What the joint model adds is the streams that inform ascertainment, which their fixed assumptions leave outside the posterior.
It adds to the projection of Chamla et al. [@chamla2026] a forecast drawn from every stream rather than from the confirmed series alone.
The confirmed cases that followed ran above their central projection and inside the interval of the joint forecast.
Genomic estimates bound the outbreak age and the early growth rate, and they enter the joint model as priors that the surveillance data then update [@mbalaplacide2026].
More generally, the model belongs to the class of multi-stream renewal models with nowcasting components, applied here to report-dated aggregates rather than to line lists [@epinow2; @lison2024nowcast].

<!-- Lessons -->

Changes in reporting were the main source of change to the model, and most of them were absorbed without a change to the latent process. <!-- RECOLLECTION: tick, strike or add -->
The disagreement between streams is itself the result to report, because the size estimate follows from how that disagreement is resolved.
Agent-drafted code needs the authors at each modelling decision, a convergence and fit-to-data gate on every change, and an independent check of each agent explanation.
The agent workflow also made engineering feasible that we would not have attempted alone, the hand-written adjoints, the wide performance searches and the release tooling. <!-- author statement, 24 Sep -->

Several defects were of a kind a human author would be unlikely to write.
Two were found by the prospective evaluation of a release and the others in review of the pull request that carried them.
The forecast extrapolated the last random-walk innovation as a fixed slope, so its intervals widened with the horizon and covered every observation. <!-- issue 606 (Sam), issue 622 (Sam), news v1.15.0 -->
Reporting-break corrections were applied in the fit but not in the scoring, so forecasts from fits fixed at each release date scored an order of magnitude out. <!-- issue 623 (Sam) -->
The posterior predictive was generated without the provincial arguments, so every case-driven stream came out short while the background-driven streams were unaffected. <!-- news v2.0.0 Fixed; how it was found is not recorded -->
A chain initialised from a fixed seed sat on a prior tail and returned the same R-hat on successive datasets. <!-- issue 671 and news v2.0.0; Sam raised the R-hat on PR 661 -->
A generation-interval prior documented as matching a published interval on the mean was much wider than that interval, and the fit pulled the mean far below the prior centre. <!-- PRs 907 and 909 -->
Each passed the tests and the in-sample checks of the release that carried it.

<!-- Further work -->

Future work could resolve the health-zone structure, ground the delays on outbreak-specific data and model the revision process directly.
A health-zone model conditioned on the provincial posterior is in development. <!-- PR 779 -->
Outbreak-specific delays could be estimated from a line list, following Akilimali et al. [@akilimali2026].
Revision could be treated as an observation process rather than as a break. <!-- CITE: revision modelling reference; the plan's placeholder key is not in refs.bib -->
A retrospective evaluation against the final counts could follow once the outbreak has ended.

The model has kept expanding and the experiments that shaped it were ad hoc, so future work could run formal experiments across settings and outbreaks. <!-- author statement, 24 Sep -->
Our own infectious disease modelling workflow [@abbott_workflow] could be applied more deliberately to test whether it improves the efficiency of agent work, measured as token use per accepted change. <!-- author statement, 24 Sep -->
How agent-driven modelling should be directed, and how a team may share work that changes this much between releases, is open. <!-- author statement, 24 Sep -->

<!-- Conclusions -->

A joint estimate of outbreak size can be produced in real time from published situation reports alone.
Its value lies in making the agreement and the conflict between surveillance streams explicit rather than in any one number.
Scoring releases against the data that arrived next found defects that review and tests did not.
We aim to support real-time size estimation from published surveillance in future outbreaks.
